title: Binary Search Tree
body:
A [[Tree]] with one invariant: for every node, everything in the left subtree is smaller and
everything in the right subtree is larger. That single rule turns searching into a sequence
of "left or right?" decisions, so each comparison throws away half the remaining tree. When
the tree is balanced that is $O(\log n)$; when it is not, it is $O(n)$ and you have written
a [[Linked List]] with extra steps.

```
        8
      /   \
     3     10
    / \      \
   1   6      14
      / \    /
     4   7  13
```

Search for 7: 7 < 8 go left, 7 > 3 go right, 7 > 6 go right, found. Three comparisons in a
tree of eight nodes.

## Operations

| Operation | Balanced | Degenerate |
|---|---|---|
| Search | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Insert | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| Delete | $O(\log n)$ | $O(n)$ |
| In-order traversal | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ |

**Search and insert** are the same walk. You descend comparing until you find the key or
fall off the bottom, and insert hangs the new node exactly where the search failed. That is
why insert costs the same as search: it *is* a search.

```java
Node insert(Node root, int key) {
    if (root == null) return new Node(key);
    if (key < root.key)      root.left  = insert(root.left, key);
    else if (key > root.key) root.right = insert(root.right, key);
    return root;                 // equal key: already here, do nothing
}
```

[[Recursion]] is the natural shape here. A subtree is a tree, so the method calls itself and
the base case is the empty subtree.

**Delete** is the awkward one, and it splits into three cases:

- *No children*: unhook it.
- *One child*: promote the child into its place.
- *Two children*: you cannot just remove it without orphaning a subtree. Replace its key
  with its **in-order successor** (the smallest key in the right subtree, found by going
  right once then left as far as possible), then delete that successor node, which by
  construction has at most one child. The in-order predecessor works just as well.

## In-order traversal gives sorted output

Left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. The BST invariant means this visits the
keys in ascending order, which is the cheapest way to get a sorted list out of a tree.

```java
void inOrder(Node n) {
    if (n == null) return;
    inOrder(n.left);
    visit(n);
    inOrder(n.right);
}
```

Pre-order (node first) is what you use to *copy* a tree, since the root arrives before its
children. Post-order (node last) is what you use to *free* one, since the children go before
the parent.

## The degenerate case

Insert 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 into an empty BST in that order:

```
1
 \
  2
   \
    3
     \
      4
       \
        5
```

Every node is a right child. Search is now a linear scan. Sorted input is not exotic, it is
the most likely input there is, so a plain BST is a trap on real data. The fix is a
[[Balanced Tree]], which rearranges the tree on insert to keep the height near $\log n$.
